entries.test: Public records of radiology staffing and AI deployment would establish whether AI had replaced any radiologist by March 9, 2025.
entries.note: The knowledge qualifier limits certainty but does not turn the factual assertion into a claim solely about his private knowledge.

entries.test: Tesla fleet and deployment records would show whether Musk delivered over a million robotaxis by his promised 2020 deadline.
entries.note: The preceding quotation supplies the promise's numerical threshold and deadline.
Calling the predictions absurd expresses an evaluative judgment.
Neither the percentage of a task nor the comparative difficulty has a shared operational meaning across these examples.

entries.test: Published research and Nobel laureates' accounts would show whether AI built in 2026 or 2027 materially assisted their scientific work.
entries.note: The years specify when the AI is built, not a deadline for its benefit to future laureates.

entries.test: Published scientific results and workflow studies would show substantial gains in scientists' productivity or capabilities from AI assistance.
entries.note: The plain reading is substantial practical assistance to scientists; no deadline is stated.
“Highly doubt” expresses likelihood rather than a firm prediction that the outcome will not happen.

entries.test: Public documentation of leading AI science systems, including Google's AI co-scientist, would establish who selected their research goals as of publication.
entries.note: The substantive assertion concerns human selection of research goals.

entries.test: Public demonstrations and research records through the end of 2026 would show whether AI had taken over choosing scientific research goals from human scientists.
entries.note: “That” refers to the preceding statement about humans choosing research goals. The 2026 horizon has not ended.

entries.test: Reproducible evaluations of AI available on March 9, 2025, on varied river-crossing puzzles would establish its reliability.
entries.note: “Current” refers to publication, not the evaluation date.
There is no shared measure for how much harder Nobel-calibre science is than driving. The separate assertion about reliable autonomous driving is checkable.

entries.test: Reproducible logic and causal-reasoning evaluations, together with independently assessed original scientific results, would show whether AI available at publication reliably possessed these capabilities.
entries.note: The plain reading concerns reliable demonstrated capabilities, despite imprecise thresholds.

entries.test: Public statements or policy documents from DOGE and its allies would show whether they invoked predictions of Nobel-level AI to justify cuts to scientific institutions.
entries.note: “I think ... will” asserts an expectation here, rather than an explicit probability. The drafter's “likely” modality understates it.
This is a rhetorical dismissal of the predictions, without a concrete claim about measurable effects on science.
